q: You apply a manifest with a Service of type LoadBalancer. kubectl get service shows EXTERNAL-IP as <pending>. What does this usually mean?
o: Azure is still provisioning the public IP for the load balancer; wait and watch the service until the IP appears
The Deployment failed to pull its image
The Service type must be ClusterIP for AKS
The cluster has no Linux node pool
e: When a LoadBalancer Service is created, AKS asks Azure to provision a public IP on the load balancer, and the EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until that finishes; the quickstart has you watch the service until the address appears. Image pull failures show on pods, ClusterIP would never get a public IP, and node OS doesn't cause a pending IP.

q: Users can't reach an app hosted in AKS. Microsoft's inside-out troubleshooting approach says to start where?
o: Check that the pod is running and the app inside it responds, using kubectl get pods and kubectl describe pod
Check the public DNS records first
Recreate the cluster's load balancer
Check the Azure subscription quota
e: The guidance for app connection issues starts inside the cluster: confirm the pod is Running and Ready and that the app responds, then work outward to the Service, ingress, and network. kubectl describe pod events reveal probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, or OOMKilled. DNS and load balancer checks come later, and quota rarely causes connectivity errors.

q: A .NET API creates a new CosmosClient for every HTTP request. Under load you see high latency and port exhaustion. What should you change?
o: Use a single CosmosClient instance for the lifetime of the application
Dispose each CosmosClient immediately after the query
Switch to strong consistency
Increase the container's RU/s
e: CosmosClient is thread-safe and manages connections and address caches, so Microsoft recommends a singleton for the application's lifetime; creating clients per request opens new connections and can exhaust ports. Disposing faster doesn't remove the connection churn, and consistency or throughput changes don't fix client-side connection problems.

q: You know both the id and the partition key value of an item. Which operation retrieves it with the lowest RU charge?
o: A point read, such as ReadItemAsync(id, new PartitionKey(pk))
SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id without a partition key
A cross-partition query with ORDER BY c._ts
Reading the change feed from the beginning
e: A point read by id and partition key goes straight to the item, and apart from the consistency level its RU charge depends only on the item's size. A query, especially without the partition key, must be planned and may fan out across partitions, which costs more. The change feed isn't a lookup mechanism.

q: Your application runs in a corporate network whose firewall only allows outbound HTTPS on port 443 to a single endpoint. Which Cosmos DB SDK connection mode should you use?
o: Gateway mode
Direct mode over TCP
Bulk mode
Session mode
e: Gateway mode sends requests over HTTPS to a single gateway endpoint, which suits networks with strict firewall rules, at the cost of an extra network hop. Direct mode connects to many backend replicas over a range of TCP ports and is faster but needs those ports open. Bulk is a throughput optimization and Session is a consistency level, not a connection mode.

q: Your API filters items by a value supplied by users. Which way of building the Cosmos DB query is recommended?
o: Use a parameterized query, for example SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.city = @city with the value passed as a parameter
Concatenate the user value into the query string
Download all items and filter in memory
Use a stored procedure for every query
e: Parameterized queries (QueryDefinition with WithParameter in .NET) keep user input out of the query text, preventing injection, and let the service reuse the query plan. String concatenation is unsafe, reading everything wastes RUs, and stored procedures are scoped to a single partition key and add no benefit here.

q: A query filters on the partition key, and the container has only a few physical partitions. Which .NET SDK feature can reduce query latency by skipping the separate query plan call?
o: Optimistic Direct Execution (EnableOptimisticDirectExecution in QueryRequestOptions)
Bulk execution mode
The change feed processor
Bounded staleness consistency
e: Optimistic Direct Execution (.NET SDK 3.38.0 and later) runs single-partition queries directly when the partition key is in the request or query, or the container has a single physical partition, and the results don't need pagination. Bulk mode is for high-volume writes, the change feed is for processing changes, and consistency doesn't affect query planning.

q: Your Cosmos DB account is replicated to West US, Central US, and East US. An app running in Central US must read from the nearest replica. What should you configure in the SDK?
o: ApplicationPreferredRegions (preferred regions) with Central US first
The partition key path
EnableContentResponseOnWrite
A larger MaxItemCount
e: Preferred regions tell the SDK which regional endpoints to use, in order, so reads go to the closest replica and fail over to the next one; Microsoft also recommends running the app in the same region as the account. The partition key, content response, and page size settings don't affect regional routing.

q: A Java service inserts large documents at high volume and never uses the item returned by createItem. How can you reduce network and CPU usage?
o: Set contentResponseOnWriteEnabled(false) on the CosmosClientBuilder
Use strong consistency
Create a new client for each write
Add a composite index
e: For workloads with heavy create payloads, the Java SDK best practices recommend turning off content response on write so the service doesn't send the full item back. Consistency and indexes don't change the response payload, and creating clients per write hurts performance.

q: Your app receives HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) responses from Cosmos DB during peak hours. What do they mean, and what is an appropriate response?
o: The request rate exceeded the provisioned RU/s; let the SDK retry after the indicated delay and, if 429s persist, increase throughput or reduce RU consumption
The partition key is invalid; recreate the container
The account has hit its storage limit; delete data
The client is using the wrong region; switch to Gateway mode
e: A 429 means the operation was rate-limited because the provisioned throughput (RU/s) was exhausted. The SDKs retry automatically using the retry-after hint, and sustained throttling calls for more RU/s or cheaper operations (for example better indexing or point reads). It isn't a partition key, storage, or region error.

q: An IoT container is partitioned by deviceId, and some devices write about 1 KB every second. Microsoft warns this design will eventually fail. Why, and what is the recommended fix?
o: A single logical partition can store at most 20 GB, so use a hierarchical partition key such as deviceId then a time value
Logical partitions are limited to 1,000 items; add more containers
Each device needs its own database
Partition keys must be numeric
e: Each logical partition, meaning all items with the same partition key value, is limited to 20 GB. A busy device can exceed that within a year, so the IoT guidance uses hierarchical partition keys (for example deviceId, then timestamp) to spread data. There's no 1,000-item limit, and partition keys don't have to be numeric.

q: Items contain a large description property that is never used in filters or ORDER BY clauses. You want to reduce the RU cost of writes. What should you change in the indexing policy?
o: Add /description/* (or /description/?) to excludedPaths while keeping /* included
Exclude /* and include only /description/?
Switch the indexing mode to lazy
Add a composite index on description
e: By default every property is indexed, and each indexed term adds write cost. Including the root and excluding unneeded paths is the recommended strategy because new properties are still indexed automatically. Including only description does the opposite of what's needed, lazy mode is obsolete, and a composite index adds even more indexing work.

q: A query uses ORDER BY c.lastName ASC, c.firstName ASC. With the default indexing policy it fails with an error about a missing index. What should you add?
o: A composite index on /lastName ASC and /firstName ASC
A range index on /lastName only
A spatial index
A vector index
e: ORDER BY on multiple properties requires a composite index whose paths and sort orders match the query. A single-property range index can't serve a multi-property sort, and spatial or vector indexes are for geospatial and similarity queries.

q: A query filters on c.category and sorts by c.price, and it consumes many RUs. Which optimization does Microsoft recommend?
o: Add a composite index on (category, price) and include both properties in the ORDER BY clause
Remove the WHERE clause and filter in the client
Switch to eventual consistency
Increase the page size to 10,000
e: For queries with both a filter and an ORDER BY, add a composite index over the filter and sort properties and include all the composite index's properties in the ORDER BY so the query uses it. Client-side filtering reads far more data, eventual consistency doesn't change query plan efficiency, and page size doesn't reduce total work.

q: A container only stores session data that expires through time-to-live, and the app never queries by any property. Which indexing policy fits best?
o: indexingMode consistent, no included paths, and /* as the only excluded path
indexingMode none with TTL enabled
Include /* and add composite indexes for every property
Exclude only /_etag/?
e: For scenarios where no property needs indexing but TTL is required, the documentation recommends consistent mode with no included paths and /* as the only excluded path, because TTL needs the indexing mode to be consistent rather than none. Indexing everything wastes write RUs, and excluding only _etag still indexes all other properties.

q: You switch to an opt-in indexing policy: /* is excluded and only /status/? and /createdAt/? are included. Queries that filter on the partition key /tenantId become expensive. Why?
o: With the exclude-root strategy, the partition key path isn't indexed unless you include it explicitly
Partition key filters never use the index
Opt-in policies disable point reads
The _ts property is no longer indexed
e: When the root path is excluded, only explicitly included paths are indexed, and the documentation notes that the partition key path isn't indexed by default with that strategy, so include it if you filter on it. Point reads don't depend on the index, and id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode.

q: Your account uses strong consistency, and read RU costs are higher than expected. What is the effect of the consistency level on reads?
o: Strong and bounded staleness reads cost about twice the RUs of the more relaxed levels
Strong reads cost the same as eventual reads
Only writes are affected by consistency
Session consistency doubles read cost
e: With strong or bounded staleness, the RU cost of any read operation, whether a point read or a query, is roughly doubled compared with session, consistent prefix, or eventual consistency. Consistency doesn't change write RU charges in this way.

q: A user updates their profile and immediately reloads the page through the same client. The app uses the default consistency level. What is guaranteed?
o: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes within the client session
Nothing; reads are eventual by default
Every client in every region sees the update instantly
The read is served from the integrated cache only
e: Session consistency is the default and guarantees that within a single session a client reads its own writes and never sees older data after newer data. Other sessions may see the update later. Strong consistency would be needed for global linearizability, and the integrated cache is a separate optional feature.

q: The account default consistency is Session. Can a single request override it, and how?
o: Yes, but only to an equal or weaker level, such as eventual or consistent prefix
Yes, to any level including strong
No, consistency can only be set at the account level
Yes, but only for writes
e: The requested consistency level for an operation must match or be weaker than the level configured on the account. You can relax a read to eventual or consistent prefix to save cost, but you can't strengthen it beyond the account default.

q: Which list shows the Cosmos DB consistency levels from strongest to weakest?
o: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual
Strong, Session, Bounded staleness, Eventual, Consistent prefix
Session, Strong, Bounded staleness, Consistent prefix, Eventual
Bounded staleness, Strong, Session, Eventual, Consistent prefix
e: Azure Cosmos DB offers five levels, ordered from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, and Eventual. Stronger levels give fresher reads at the cost of higher latency, lower availability, or more RUs.

q: Query metrics show Retrieved Document Count far higher than Output Document Count, and the query costs 400 RUs. What is the most likely cause?
o: A property used in the filter isn't indexed, so many documents are loaded and filtered after retrieval
The client uses Direct mode
The container uses session consistency
The query uses a parameter
e: When far more documents are retrieved than returned, the engine is loading documents to evaluate filters it couldn't answer from the index. The troubleshooting guide's example removes an excluded path so the filter becomes indexed, dropping the charge sharply. Connection mode, session consistency, and parameters don't cause this pattern.

q: A read-heavy app repeatedly reads the same large items and runs the same expensive queries. You want cache hits to cost zero RUs without writing your own caching layer. What should you use?
o: The Cosmos DB integrated cache through a dedicated gateway
Strong consistency
A composite index
The change feed processor
e: The integrated cache, accessed through a dedicated gateway, serves point reads and queries from memory, and cache hits have an RU charge of zero, which suits read-heavy workloads with repeated reads. Strong consistency increases read cost, a composite index only helps specific queries, and the change feed processes writes.

q: What determines the RU charge of a point read, besides the consistency level?
o: The size of the item retrieved
The number of indexed properties
The number of physical partitions
The length of the partition key path
e: The cost optimization guide states that the only factor affecting the RU charge of a point read, apart from consistency, is the size of the item; for example, a 1 KB item costs about 1 RU. Indexing affects writes and queries, and partition count doesn't change a point read's cost.

q: You want to store 1,536-dimension embeddings in Cosmos DB for NoSQL and query them by similarity. Which two definitions are required when you create the container? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.
o: A vector embedding policy that defines the path, data type, distance function, and dimensions
A vector index (for example diskANN) on the embedding path in the indexing policy
A composite index on the embedding path
A unique key on the embedding path
e: Vector search in Cosmos DB for NoSQL needs a container vector embedding policy, describing each vector path's data type, dimensions, and distance function, plus a vector index entry in the indexing policy. Composite indexes and unique keys apply to scalar properties and can't index embeddings.

q: Which query returns the five items most similar to a query embedding passed as @embedding?
o: SELECT TOP 5 c.title, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @embedding) AS score FROM c ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @embedding)
SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c WHERE c.embedding = @embedding
SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c ORDER BY c.embedding DESC
SELECT TOP 5 c.title FROM c WHERE CONTAINS(c.embedding, @embedding)
e: VectorDistance computes the similarity between a stored vector and the query vector, and ordering by it returns the nearest neighbors using the configured vector index and distance function. Equality, plain ORDER BY on an array, and CONTAINS don't perform similarity search.

q: You try to create a flat vector index for 1,536-dimension embeddings and the request is rejected. Which index types support this dimension count?
o: quantizedFlat or diskANN, which support up to 4,096 dimensions
Only flat, after reducing dimensions to 2,048
A composite index
A spatial index
e: The flat index supports at most 505 dimensions, while quantizedFlat and diskANN support up to 4,096. Reducing to 2,048 still exceeds the flat limit, and composite and spatial indexes don't index vectors.

q: Which requirement applies to the quantizedFlat and diskANN vector index types in Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
o: At least 1,000 vectors must be inserted
The container must use strong consistency
Vectors must have exactly 1,536 dimensions
The container must use serverless capacity
e: The documentation states that the quantizedFlat and diskANN indexes require at least 1,000 vectors to be inserted. They support up to 4,096 dimensions, work with any consistency level, and aren't tied to a capacity mode.

q: Each physical partition of your container will hold about 20,000 vectors, and you want a good balance of recall, latency, and cost. Which vector index type does Microsoft recommend?
o: quantizedFlat
diskANN with vectorIndexShardKey
flat
No vector index; use full scans
e: quantizedFlat is recommended when roughly 50,000 or fewer vectors are indexed per physical partition (or search scope). diskANN, optionally sharded by partition key, is the choice for larger partitions. flat is exact but limited to 505 dimensions and slow at scale, and full scans cost far more RUs.

q: A multitenant container stores millions of vectors, and queries always filter by tenantId, the partition key. Several tenants have more than 50,000 vectors. Which configuration does Microsoft recommend?
o: A diskANN index with vectorIndexShardKey set to the partition key path
A flat index
A quantizedFlat index without any shard key
A separate container per vector
e: For larger partitions (more than 50,000 vectors), the performance tips recommend diskANN with vectorIndexShardKey set to the partition key path, so each tenant's vectors get their own index shard and filtered searches stay fast. flat doesn't scale, quantizedFlat is aimed at smaller scopes, and a container per vector is impractical.

q: Inserting documents that contain large embeddings consumes more RUs than expected. The indexing policy includes /* and also defines a diskANN vector index on /embedding. What should you change?
o: Add the vector path /embedding/* to excludedPaths so it isn't also indexed as a regular property
Remove the vector embedding policy
Switch to strong consistency
Add a composite index on /embedding
e: Microsoft recommends excluding vector paths from the regular included paths, because indexing every array element as a normal property adds significant write cost while the vector index already covers similarity search. Removing the embedding policy breaks vector search, and consistency or composite indexes don't reduce this cost.

q: Which distance functions can you set in a Cosmos DB vector embedding policy?
o: cosine, dotproduct, and euclidean
manhattan, hamming, and jaccard
cosine only
levenshtein and cosine
e: The vector embedding policy supports cosine, dot product, and Euclidean distance functions, and the TypeScript quickstart compares rankings produced by all three. The other options list metrics that Cosmos DB vector search doesn't offer.

q: A small reference dataset has 2,000 vectors of 384 dimensions, and the business requires exact nearest-neighbor results (100 percent recall). Which index type fits?
o: flat
diskANN
quantizedFlat
No index; approximate search is always exact
e: The flat index performs exact kNN search with 100 percent recall and supports up to 505 dimensions, so 384-dimension vectors fit. quantizedFlat and diskANN compress vectors or use approximate search, trading a little recall for speed. Approximate search isn't exact by definition.

q: Your RAG app must return the 10 most similar support articles, but only those in the product category the user selected. How should you write the query?
o: Combine a WHERE filter with vector ordering: SELECT TOP 10 ... FROM c WHERE c.category = @category ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)
Run the vector query for TOP 10, then remove other categories in the client
Create one container per category
Store the category inside the embedding vector
e: Cosmos DB lets you combine regular filters with VectorDistance ordering in the same query, so the top results already respect the metadata filter. Filtering after a TOP 10 can return fewer than 10 relevant results, a container per category is unnecessary, and embeddings can't carry exact metadata filters.

q: Your embedding model returns 1,536-dimension vectors, but the vector embedding policy declares 768 dimensions. What should you do?
o: Make the policy's dimensions match the model's output size
Truncate every vector to 768 values before inserting it
Switch the distance function to dotproduct
Leave it as it is; dimensions are only a hint
e: The vector embedding policy defines the dimensions of the vectors at the path, and stored and query vectors must match it and the embedding model. Truncating vectors corrupts their meaning, and the distance function doesn't change the dimension requirement.

q: Which four components make up the Cosmos DB change feed processor?
o: The monitored container, the lease container, the host (compute instance), and the delegate (your code)
The source container, the dead-letter queue, the scheduler, and the trigger
The monitored container, an Event Grid topic, a webhook, and a function
The lease container, a Service Bus queue, a timer, and an estimator
e: The change feed processor has a monitored container that generates the change feed, a lease container that stores state and coordinates workers, hosts that run the processor, and a delegate that handles each batch of changes. Dead-letter queues, Event Grid, and Service Bus aren't part of it.

q: You run three instances of the same change feed processor to keep up with writes. How should they be configured so they share the work?
o: Same processor name and lease container, and a different instance name on each host
A different lease container on each host
A different processor name on each host
Only one instance can run; the others must be standby
e: Instances with the same lease configuration (processor name and lease container) form one deployment and split the leases between them, while each instance needs a unique instance name. Different lease containers or processor names would make each instance process every change independently.

q: You need two independent jobs to process the same container's change feed: one updates a search index and one sends emails. To save cost you want one lease container. Is that possible?
o: Yes; use a different processor name for each job so their leases don't collide
No; every processor needs its own lease container
Yes, but only if both jobs run on the same host
No; a container's change feed can be read by only one processor
e: A lease container can be shared as long as each logical job uses its own processor name, so its leases are tracked separately. Several processors can read the same change feed independently, and they don't need to run on the same host.

q: You suspect your change feed processor is falling behind the write rate. Which tool measures how far behind it is?
o: The change feed estimator, which compares the leases' state with the latest changes
Cosmos DB query metrics
The Azure Activity log
A composite index
e: The change feed estimator measures the difference between the last processed item, recorded in the lease container, and the latest change in the monitored container, and reports it to a delegate (push model) or on demand. Query metrics, the Activity log, and indexes don't show processing lag.

q: You are getting started with the change feed and want the simplest way to run code whenever items are created or modified, with leases handled for you. What does Microsoft recommend?
o: An Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger
A custom polling loop that queries _ts every second
An Event Grid subscription on the Cosmos DB account
A timer-triggered function that reads the whole container
e: Azure Functions is described as the simplest option and is recommended for most change feed scenarios; the Cosmos DB trigger uses the change feed processor and a lease container behind the scenes. Polling by _ts and full reads waste RUs, and Event Grid doesn't deliver per-item change feed events.

q: You read the change feed with the pull model and want to switch to the change feed processor without reprocessing changes. Can you convert your stored continuation token into a lease?
o: No; continuation tokens and leases both act as bookmarks, but they can't be converted into each other
Yes; paste the token into the lease container
Yes; the SDK converts it automatically on startup
Only if both use the same processor name
e: The pull model's continuation tokens and the processor's lease container both record the last processed point, but the documentation states you can't convert continuation tokens to a lease or vice versa. Plan the cut-over, for example by starting the processor from a point in time, and make processing idempotent.

q: A change feed consumer must remove items from a search index when they are deleted in Cosmos DB, but deletes never arrive in the default (latest version) change feed. What is a common solution?
o: Use a soft-delete flag (for example isDeleted: true) and set a TTL so the item is removed after the consumer sees the update
Read the change feed from the beginning every hour
Use strong consistency
Enable a composite index on _ts
e: The latest version mode of the change feed captures inserts and updates but not deletes. A soft-delete update is captured as a change that the consumer can act on, and TTL then removes the item. Rereading the feed or changing consistency and indexing doesn't surface deletes.

q: Your delegate occasionally throws an exception because a downstream API is unavailable. What should you assume about delivery, and how should you write the handler?
o: Failed batches are retried, so changes can be delivered more than once; make processing idempotent
Each change is delivered exactly once even if the delegate fails
Failed changes are moved to a dead-letter queue automatically
The processor stops permanently on the first error
e: The change feed processor handles errors by retrying changes that weren't processed correctly, so a batch can be seen again and handlers should be idempotent. There's no exactly-once guarantee and no built-in dead-letter queue, and the processor doesn't stop permanently on a single exception.

q: Where can the lease container for a change feed processor be located?
o: In the same Cosmos DB account as the monitored container or in a separate account
Only in the same database as the monitored container
Only in an Azure Storage account
Only in Azure Table storage
e: The lease container stores processor state and coordinates workers, and it can live in the same account as the monitored container or in a different account. It is a Cosmos DB container, not an Azure Storage resource.

q: You create an Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger, but no lease container exists yet. What does the trigger need?
o: A lease container, which you either create yourself or let the trigger create (CreateLeaseContainerIfNotExists)
A Service Bus queue to store checkpoints
A Blob container to store leases
Nothing; the trigger keeps its state in memory
e: The Cosmos DB trigger is built on the change feed processor and needs a lease container to track progress; you can point it at an existing container or let it create one. Checkpoints aren't stored in Service Bus or Blob storage, and in-memory state would be lost on restart and couldn't coordinate scaled-out instances.
